title: Ines and the Tide
premise: Ivo Winterbourne, granddaughter of a lighthouse keeper and a part-time novelist, has spent a decade avoiding the coastal town of Gullwrack and the man she once loved. When a snowstorm strands her there with Theo Marsh — her former writing partner, rival for the same book prize, and the best mistake of her twenties — old wounds and old tenderness resurface faster than either can rationalize. As the tide cuts the causeway and her grandmother's memory begins to fail, Ivo must decide whether the career that saved her is worth the person who finally sees her clearly. She chooses love, but on her own terms: they write the next book together, and she keeps the lighthouse.
about_author: Silas Underhill is the pen name of a former tide-chart clerk who spent seven winters living in decommissioned lightstations along the northern coast before turning to fiction. Their novels are known for salt-weathered romances in which love arrives the way weather does — suddenly, and without permission.

chapters.title: The Causeway Closes
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Returning to Gullwrack to settle her grandmother's care, Ivo intends to stay three days, sign papers, and leave before anyone recognizes her. The last ferry cancels; the causeway closes behind her. The beat is reluctant homecoming — the ache of a place that remembers you better than you remember it.

chapters.title: Snow at the Door
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The storm hits early. A car slides off the coast road and out of it steps Theo Marsh, her old writing partner and the man who broke her heart at twenty-four, now her direct rival for the Whitmore Prize. Snowbound in her grandmother's cottage, they circle each other with brittle courtesy. The beat is charged, unwilling proximity.

chapters.title: What the Lighthouse Kept
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Trapped indoors, Theo finds Ivo's unfinished manuscript and reads it without meaning to — and discovers she has written their entire history into it, including the part he never apologized for. He begins drafting a letter he may never send. The beat is guilt sharpening into longing.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Weather
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Her grandmother, Marren, mistakes Theo for a boy from decades past and serves him tea as if he belongs there. Ivo watches Theo play along gently, and something in her chest loosens. The beat is the first thaw — found family forming around a fading memory.

chapters.title: The Prize and the Price
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A phone call reveals the Whitmore shortlist: only one of them can win, and Theo's publisher expects him to bury Ivo's book in the press round. He stalls, then lies badly. When Ivo finds the draft press statement, the thaw freezes over. The beat is betrayal re-staged, history threatening to repeat.

chapters.title: Low Water, Old Wounds
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo walks the exposed flats alone and remembers the night everything ended — the rejected draft, the cruel review, the kiss that came too late. Theo follows her out onto the sand and, for the first time, tells her the whole truth about that winter. The beat is raw honesty without absolution yet.

chapters.title: Marren's Last Clear Day
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Marren has a lucid morning and, seeing the two of them circling, tells them plainly that she spent forty years waiting for a man the tide took, and that waiting is a choice, not a fate. She gives Ivo her old logbooks. The beat is a blessing and a warning in one breath; stakes become mortal and finite.

chapters.title: The Withdrawal
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo withdraws from the Whitmore Prize, sacrificing the career that rescued him from ruin, and sends Ivo the letter he wrote in Chapter Three — his full confession, in her grandmother's borrowed handwriting style, because he knows she'll actually read that. The beat is the grand gesture, but quiet and costly rather than theatrical.

chapters.title: Storm Surge
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The storm peaks; the lighthouse lamp fails and Marren wanders out toward the water. Ivo and Theo find her together, and in the wind and flood Ivo finally says what she withheld at twenty-four. The beat is the climax — fear, fury, and love colliding in the dark, and the choice made with time running out.

chapters.title: Spring Tide
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, epilogue in spring. The prize goes to neither of them; instead, their co-written novel — built from Marren's logbooks — is accepted. Ivo keeps the lighthouse as a writing retreat, Theo moves in with his typewriter, and Marren sits in the lamp room calling them both by the right names at last. The beat is belonging, chosen and kept.
